# C11 Atomics and Memory Order

## Thesis

**`_Atomic` variables and `memory_order_*`** are how C11 expresses shared-memory concurrency without guessing what the compiler and CPU will reorder. A plain `int` counter with two threads is a data race; `atomic_fetch_add` is not. This chapter builds a tiny two-thread counter and names the memory orders you actually need.

## Mental model

```text
  atomic_int counter;
  atomic_fetch_add_explicit(&counter, 1, memory_order_relaxed);
        │                         │
        │                         └─ how visible to other threads
        └─ RMW that cannot tear
```

- **`memory_order_relaxed`**: atomicity only; no ordering with other memory.
- **`memory_order_acquire` / `release`**: pair a \producer store with a consumer load.
- **`memory_order_seq_cst`**: default when you call the non-`_explicit` APIs; strongest and usually fine until a profile says otherwise.

## Worked example

Verified with **GCC 14.2**, `-std=c11 -pthread`.

```c
/* atomics.c */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <threads.h>
#include <stdatomic.h>

atomic_int counter = 0;

int worker(void *arg) {
  (void)arg;
  for (int i = 0; i < 100000; i++)
    atomic_fetch_add_explicit(&counter, 1, memory_order_relaxed);
  return 0;
}

int main(void) {
  thrd_t t1, t2;
  thrd_create(&t1, worker, NULL);
  thrd_create(&t2, worker, NULL);
  thrd_join(t1, NULL);
  thrd_join(t2, NULL);
  printf("counter=%d\n", atomic_load(&counter));
  printf("memory_order_seq_cst=%d relaxed=%d\n",
         (int)memory_order_seq_cst, (int)memory_order_relaxed);
  return 0;
}
```

```bash
gcc -O2 -std=c11 atomics.c -pthread -o atomics && ./atomics
```

Observed on this box:

```text
counter=200000
memory_order_seq_cst=5 relaxed=0
```

Two hundred thousand increments land exactly — no lost updates. The enum values are implementation-defined integers; do not hard-code them.

## Trap

**Mixing plain loads/stores of an `_Atomic` with non-atomic access to the same object.** Once a variable is `_Atomic`, every access goes through the atomic API (or `_Atomic`-qualified lvalues). Also: `volatile` is not a substitute for atomics.

## Boring rule

Start with the non-`_explicit` operations (`atomic_fetch_add`, `atomic_load`, `atomic_store`) — they are sequentially consistent. Reach for `relaxed` only when a shared counter truly needs no ordering, and document why.

## Try this

1. Drop `_Atomic` and use a plain `int`; run under ThreadSanitizer (`-fsanitize=thread`) and read the race report.
2. Replace `relaxed` with `seq_cst` and confirm the count is unchanged (correctness) while thinking about fence cost on weakly ordered CPUs.
3. Build a release/acquire hand-off: thread A stores a payload then `atomic_store_explicit(&ready, 1, memory_order_release)`; thread B spins with `acquire`.
